title: T1102.002 — Web Service - Bidirectional Communication
subtitle: Watch one full tasking round trip: a command travels in through a chat platform, results travel out the same way, and the SOC watches both.

steps.title: Implant installed with an embedded bot token
steps.caption: A user opens a phishing attachment, and a dropper installs the implant on the workstation. The implant carries a chat bot token in its configuration file or memory.
steps.defender: EDR sees the process tree and a new scheduled task; the proxy still shows nothing unusual.

steps.title: Attacker sends a task through the chat platform
steps.caption: From a laptop far away, the operator types a command into the bot chat, for example "screenshot and collect recent documents". The platform stores the message as an update for the bot.
steps.defender: nothing on your network yet; the message sits on the platform waiting to be polled.

steps.title: Malware polls getUpdates and receives the task
steps.caption: The implant calls the platform API every 30 seconds with a small request. The next poll returns the pending task. The request is tiny; the rhythm is regular.
steps.defender: proxy logs show small, evenly spaced POST/GET requests to a chat API domain from a workstation - the first visible beacon.

steps.title: Malware executes the task
steps.caption: It takes a screenshot, lists directories, and copies selected files into a temp folder. All of this happens inside the host.
steps.defender: EDR notices the beacon process spawning system tools, touching many files, and writing to a staging directory.

steps.title: Malware uploads results through the same API
steps.caption: The implant sends the screenshot and collected files back with upload calls (sendDocument-style POST with multipart data). Traffic out is much larger than the polls in.
steps.defender: proxy shows a big outbound POST to the same chat API - bytes far above any normal poll.

steps.title: Attacker downloads the results
steps.caption: The operator opens the chat, sees the new documents, and pulls them down from the platform. The attacker's own IP never appears in your logs; only the platform does.
steps.defender: on SaaS/audit side, a new document appears in the bot's storage; on your side, only the outbound upload was visible.

steps.title: The loop continues with the next task
steps.caption: The attacker sends another command; the next poll picks it up. Requests in, results out, again and again - this is the bidirectional pattern. Over hours the rhythm stays regular even as content changes.
steps.defender: a 24-hour proxy timeline shows dozens of identical-size polls plus periodic upload spikes: the classic C2+exfil signature.

detection.label: Alert raised
detection.detail: The SOC has enough evidence to open an incident.

steps.title: SOC responds
steps.caption: CASB flags uploads from a server identity; EDR shows which process made the API calls. The team revokes the bot token by reporting the bot to the platform, blocks the API domain for that host group, and isolates the workstation.
steps.defender: containment breaks the loop: polls stop, uploads stop, and the implant can no longer hear orders.
